newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO ministers to push Russia on military swaps.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers to push Russia on military swaps.

text.p: NATO defence ministers meet in Brussels this week to review internal alliance reform, rubber stamp a new peace force for Bosnia and try to push Russia to agree an exchange of military liasion officers, .

The 16 alliance ministers, meeting in Brussels on Tuesday and Wednesday, will also confer with some 27 partners from the rest of Europe to examine planned joint military exercises and other ways of boosting ties.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov will attend the meeting on Wednesday but will also hold a separate meeting with the 16 allies on ways to make tangible progress on building a new relationship between the former enemies.

Last week, Russia agreed to open talks on a new charter or treaty to govern all aspects of the relationship between the former Cold War foes despite deep and lingering hostility over the alliance's plans to expand into former communist Europe.

NATO, keen to have the deal with Russia ready for a special enlargement summit in Madrid next July, wants to push ahead with plans to exchange military officers at the top levels of NATO's and Moscow's political and military commands.

Those plans, which have effectively been on the table for almost a year while Russia evolved its position on future NATO ties, build on close cooperation the two sides have forged over Moscow's participation in the alliance's Bosnian peace force.

NATO and troop contributing countries outside the alliance, including Russia, have agreed to replace the current Implementation Force (IFOR) with a new, smaller Stabilisation Force (SFOR) when its mandate expires on December 20.

SFOR, agreed by alliance foreign ministers last week, will be authorised by a U.N. Security Council resolution later this week. Defence ministers will take one last look at the military's plans, including its rules of engagement.
"Russia has been involved in the planning of SFOR almost from day one, at a very close and high level. This has played an enormous part in changing Moscow's perceptions of NATO," said one NATO envoy.
NATO hopes Rodionov will now agree to exchange military personnel on a permanent basis and set up information and liaison offices at their respective headquarters.

The alliance ministers are also due to take stock of plans for a widescale reform of NATO command structures, considered essential if enlargement is to go ahead and the alliance be equipped for a more flexible post-Cold War role.

The highly complex process of overhauling structures originally designed to meet attack from the Soviet Union has recently been overshadowed by a French-U.S. row over the future of NATO's key southern command.
France is demanding that Washington hand over the top command post to a European as part of attempts to create a more distinct European identity within the U.S.-dominated alliance.

Paris argues the issue goes to the heart of the European Security Defence Identity (ESDI) -- another key plank of the reform process -- and says it could prevent France returning to the alliance's military wing, which it quit in 1966.
Washington flatly refuses to hand over the command which controls the Mediterranean and the U.S. Navy's Sixth Fleet.

"The French are out of their minds on this. Anyone who thinks Congress -- and this Congress in particular -- will allow a foreigner to control American troops is simply out of the loop," said one U.S. defence analyst.
The issue will not be resolved in the Brussels talks, but the ministers will look at broader refrom questions, most pertinently how many strategic and regional commands to retain.
Pushed by budget constraints, virtually every member state is in favour of eliminating some commands but no-one wants to lose its own posts and influence.
